Advisory.Description:
### Summary
The recursive traversal engines behind WordNetCorpusReader's Synset.tree() and Synset.acyclic_tree() have no maximum call-depth safeguard and default to unlimited depth. They guard against literal cycles, but not against a long, genuinely acyclic relation chain — which exhausts the Python call stack the same way as the sibling DependencyGraph finding I reported separately. Real-world exploitability requires the host application to load a custom/foreign WordNet-format lexical resource rather than NLTK's bundled default corpus — flagging that narrower scope honestly up front since it affects severity, not validity.

### Details
`nltk/util.py`'s `acyclic_depth_first()` (~lines 471-541) and `acyclic_branches_depth_first()` (~lines 544-625) recurse once per graph edge, default to `depth=-1` ("unlimited"), and guard against re-visiting the same node via an explicit `traversed` set (hence "acyclic") — but that set only prevents literal cycles, it never bounds how many *distinct* nodes a single call chain may pass through before returning.

`Synset.tree(rel, depth=-1)` (`nltk/corpus/reader/wordnet.py`, ~line 664) calls the recursive `acyclic_branches_depth_first`. There is also a third, easy-to-miss method: `Synset.acyclic_tree()`, a vestigial class-attribute alias for `acyclic_depth_first` — also genuinely recursive and vulnerable.

**Important correction to an earlier draft of this finding:** `Synset.closure(rel, depth=-1)` (~line 609) does **not** share this bug — it actually calls `acyclic_breadth_first()`, a completely different, iterative queue/deque-based function with no recursion at all. I verified this directly: feeding both `acyclic_breadth_first` and the real `Synset.closure()` a 20,000-node genuinely-acyclic chain produces zero crash, while `acyclic_depth_first`/`acyclic_branches_depth_first`/`Synset.tree()`/`Synset.acyclic_tree()` crash reliably at ~1000-1500 nodes on the identical data. Only `.tree()` and `.acyclic_tree()` are affected — not `.closure()`.

This is the same CWE-674 pattern already hardened elsewhere in the codebase (`MAX_TREE_DEPTH` in `tree/tree.py`, `MAX_DEPTH` in `featstruct.py`, `MAX_PARSE_DEPTH` in `logic.py`, `MAX_TABLEAU_DEPTH` in `tableau.py`, `MAX_DECODE_DEPTH` in `jsontags.py`, added by a commit whose message explicitly enumerates the sinks it covers) — but that hardening pass never reached `nltk/util.py` or `wordnet.py`.

**Honest scope-limiting fact:** I exhaustively measured the maximum possible traversal depth across the entire official, bundled WordNet 3.0 corpus (what the overwhelming majority of real deployments use) for every relation NLTK exposes to `tree()`: hypernyms/hyponyms max depth = 18 (across all 74,374 noun synsets); `also_sees` (a relation whose graph isn't curated to stay as shallow as the taxonomy) max eccentricity = 41, largest connected component = 824 nodes; `similar_tos` max eccentricity = 1; entailments/causes/verb_groups/member_holonyms/member_meronyms/attributes all ≤ 11. Every one of these is roughly 25-60x below the ~1000-node crash threshold — there is no word or relation an attacker could pick against the standard bundled corpus that reaches anywhere near a crash. `nltk.app.wordnet_app`, NLTK's own bundled reference consumer, only ever calls `.tree()` with the safe hypernym relation.

Real-world exploitability therefore strictly requires the host application to load a custom/foreign WordNet-format lexical resource — a legitimate, documented, `WordNetCorpusReader`-supported usage, but a comparatively uncommon one — and then call `.tree()`/`.acyclic_tree()` (not `.closure()`) with the default unbounded depth.

### PoC
Generated a syntactically valid, minimal, real Princeton-WordNet-DB-format lexical database (`data.noun`/`index.noun`/`lexnames`/etc., with correct byte-offset-indexed synset records) encoding a 1500-node strictly-linear (genuinely acyclic) hypernym chain. Loaded it via the real, unmodified `WordNetCorpusReader(root, None)`, obtained a real `Synset`, and called the real, documented, public `synset.tree(lambda s: s.hypernyms())` — crashed with an uncaught `RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded`, as did `synset.acyclic_tree(...)`. `synset.closure(...)` on the identical data returned cleanly (1499 nodes, no crash), confirming the closure()/tree() distinction above.

### Impact
An application that loads a custom WordNet-format lexical resource (e.g. a domain-specific or community-contributed WordNet, which `WordNetCorpusReader` is explicitly designed to support) and calls `.tree()`/`.acyclic_tree()` with an attacker-influenced or simply not-officially-curated relation/resource can be crashed via an unhandled `RecursionError` from a single long-but-acyclic relation chain. Narrower reach than a bundled-default-corpus bug, but a real, working, unpatched gap in the same CWE-674 family the project actively hardens elsewhere.

Suggested fix: apply the same `MAX_TREE_DEPTH`-style depth guard to `acyclic_depth_first()`/`acyclic_branches_depth_first()` (or reuse the existing `Tree` constant/pattern directly).


## Fix status (2026-09-28)

Status: MERGED on develop (unreleased; v3.10.3 of 2026-08-12 predates the fix).

Fix commit: 0e474a7d7 "Merge commit from fork" (2026-08-26, merged on develop from this advisory's temporary private fork): nltk/util.py gains MAX_RECURSION_DEPTH=500 for the acyclic traversal helpers behind Synset.tree() and acyclic_tree(), with nltk/test/unit/test_wordnet_recursion.py and the probe.

Probe: nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_8846_p9w9_5frf.py; verdict on develop 2fa3f48fe: FIXED (depth cap prevents recursion overflow).

Release: none yet; no release tag contains 0e474a7d7.
Advisory.Summary: Natural Language Toolkit (NLTK): Uncontrolled recursion (crash DoS) in Synset.tree()/acyclic_tree() via WordNet relation traversal
